periods.activity_title: Tracing the Godavari: Map Reading and River Geography
periods.section_ref: Where I Begin, Where I Flow
periods.textbook_anchor: Where I Begin, Where I Flow — Identify states Godavari flows through, name a dam and wildlife sanctuary along it, and name tributaries that join it (p. 22)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook map of the Godavari river system (p. 22)

time_bands.activity: The teacher reads aloud the opening poem from the textbook in which the Godavari narrates its own journey. Students listen with textbooks closed, then share what images or places the poem brought to mind.

Students open Textbook p. 22 and study the river map. They trace the Godavari's path from Trimbakeshwar in the Western Ghats to the Bay of Bengal, noting the states it passes through and marking any dams and wildlife sanctuaries visible on the map.

Students write responses to the three map questions on Textbook p. 22 in their notebooks: the states the river flows through, a dam and wildlife sanctuary along its course, and the smaller rivers that join it as tributaries.

Pairs share their answers aloud. The teacher draws out the detail that Godavari is also called Dakshina Ganga and that pilgrims gather at Nashik for the Godavari Pushkaram festival, inviting students to connect the river's name and festival to any rivers or water festivals they know from their own region.

periods.implied_lo: Students can extract geographical information about a river system from a map and record its key features.
periods.section_context: Godavari river, Trimbakeshwar source, Western Ghats, tributaries, Bay of Bengal, states along the route, dam, wildlife sanctuary, Dakshina Ganga, Godavari Pushkaram festival, Nashik.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'If you were the river, which part of the journey would you find most exciting — the mountain beginning, the forest middle, or the sea end?' This keeps the first-person river voice alive and helps students stay inside the section's narrative register.

periods.activity_title: Perennial or Seasonal? Classifying Rivers and Their Living World
periods.textbook_anchor: The Life I Hold — Understand the difference between perennial and seasonal rivers and identify the wildlife and ecosystems Godavari supports (p. 22)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook illustration of Godavari forest and delta ecosystems

time_bands.activity: The teacher poses a warm question: 'Does every river flow all year long, or do some go quiet in summer?' Students share ideas freely. The teacher introduces the terms perennial and seasonal without defining them, letting students attempt definitions from the words themselves.

Students read the section in the textbook. They then discuss in pairs: Why would a river that flows all year be more useful to people and animals than one that dries up in summer? Groups share reasoning with the class.

The teacher lists the living things named in the section — tiger, barking deer, Indian golden gecko, red sandalwood trees, Coringa Mangrove Forests — and students discuss which of these could survive if the river became seasonal. They record a two-column table in their notebooks: 'Needs perennial water' vs 'Might manage with seasonal water.'

Brief closing circle: each student names one creature or plant from the section and says one thing the river does for it. The teacher notes that the river's mouth — the delta — is where freshwater meets the sea, creating a unique habitat.

periods.implied_lo: Students can distinguish between perennial and seasonal water systems and explain how year-round flow supports specific wildlife and ecosystems.
periods.section_context: Perennial river, seasonal river, Godavari forests, tiger, barking deer, Indian golden gecko, red sandalwood trees, Godavari delta, Coringa Mangrove Forests, freshwater meeting the sea.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask students whether any river or stream near their home or village dries up in summer — this connects the perennial/seasonal distinction to lived experience and opens space for local ecological knowledge without labelling it as such.

periods.activity_title: Why People Settle Near Rivers: Reasoning from Evidence
periods.section_ref: The Many Ways I Support Lives
periods.textbook_anchor: The Many Ways I Support Lives — Explain why people have always built homes near rivers or water bodies (p. 24)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook illustration of settlements along the Godavari

time_bands.activity: Students look at the textbook illustration of settlements along the Godavari on Textbook p. 24. Without reading the text, they note three things they can see people doing near the river. Observations are shared aloud.

Students write their response to the question on Textbook p. 24: 'Since ancient times, people have always built their homes near rivers or water bodies — can you guess why?' They then read the section text to check and extend their reasoning.

Class discussion: students list the specific ways Godavari supports people — drinking, cooking, washing, irrigation through canals and pipes, industrial use. The teacher asks which of these uses existed in ancient times and which are more recent, prompting thinking about how human needs have changed while the river remains constant.

Students write responses to the questions on Textbook p. 25: three ways people depend on Godavari, and the occupations people near it pursue. Responses are compared in pairs before a few are shared with the class.

periods.implied_lo: Students can identify reasons why human settlements form near water systems and list the ways a river supports daily life and livelihoods.
periods.section_context: Ancient settlements near rivers, drinking water, cooking water, washing, irrigation, canals, pipes, industrial use, Godavari, fishing, agriculture, ecotourism.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Pose: 'If the Godavari suddenly stopped flowing for one month, which of the things we just listed would be affected first?' This near-to-far reasoning deepens students' understanding of dependency without requiring them to leave the section's content.

periods.activity_title: Rivers and Farming: Crops, Water Sources, and a Classroom Poster
periods.section_ref: The Many Ways I Support Lives
periods.textbook_anchor: The Many Ways I Support Lives — Make a poster showing all the ways rivers help people, including drawings of homes, farms, boats, and fishermen (p. 26)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook illustration of rice cultivation near the Godavari (p. 26)

time_bands.activity: Students open Textbook p. 26 and identify the crops visible in the illustration near the Godavari. They write a short response: 'Which crops grow in your region, and where does the irrigation water come from?' Responses are shared in pairs, surfacing regional variety in crops and water sources.

The class compiles a shared list on the board of all the ways rivers help people, drawn from the section and from the students' own regional experience. The teacher ensures homes, farms, boats, fishing, and ecotourism are all represented.

Students make a poster on their drawing sheet or in their notebooks illustrating all the ways rivers help people, following the task on Textbook p. 26. They include drawings of homes, farms, boats, fishermen, and any other uses from the board list. Labels in their own words accompany each drawing.
A quick gallery walk: students hold up or place their posters for neighbours to see. One student names the most surprising use of a river that appeared on a classmate's poster.

periods.implied_lo: Students can represent multiple human uses of a river system visually and through labelled drawings, connecting textbook content to their own regional context.
periods.section_context: Rice cultivation near Godavari, crops in students' own regions, irrigation water sources, homes near rivers, farms, boats, fishermen, ecotourism, multiple river uses.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Circulate during the poster-making and ask each student to include at least one use from their own region alongside the textbook examples — this ensures the poster is personally grounded, not a copy of the illustration.

periods.activity_title: Dam Trade-Offs: Benefits, Displacement, and Reasoned Judgement
periods.section_ref: Dams—Storing My Water, Changing My Flow
periods.textbook_anchor: Dams—Storing My Water, Changing My Flow — Identify problems that arise after a dam is built and suggest how they can be solved (p. 27)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook diagram or image of a dam and reservoir (p. 27)

time_bands.activity: The teacher asks: 'If you could store all the rain that falls in the monsoon and use it in summer, what would you use to store it?' Students brainstorm freely. The teacher introduces the idea of a dam as a structure that does exactly this — blocks river flow to build a reservoir.

Students read the section on Textbook p. 27. They identify: (a) what a dam provides — stored water for drinking, irrigation, and electricity; (b) what it costs — land flooded, wildlife displaced, people relocated. They record these in a two-column table: Benefits | Problems.

Small groups discuss the question from Textbook p. 27: 'What problems can arise after a dam is built? How can they be solved?' Each group appoints a speaker to share their reasoning. The teacher notes that India has more than 900 dams and that this trade-off is real and ongoing.

Students write their individual response to the textbook question in their notebooks, drawing on the group discussion. The teacher closes by asking: 'Is a dam always good or always bad, or does it depend — and on what?' This is left as an open thinking prompt, not resolved.

periods.implied_lo: Students can identify the benefits and costs of a human-made water storage structure and reason about trade-offs between development and displacement.
periods.section_context: Dams, reservoir, blocked river flow, stored water, drinking water, irrigation, electricity generation, flooded land, wildlife displacement, human displacement, 900+ dams in India.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: If students know of a dam in their state, invite them to name it — this anchors the trade-off discussion in a real case. Ask: 'Who benefits most from the dam, and who bears the biggest cost?' to push toward analysis rather than simple approval or disapproval.

periods.activity_title: What Goes Into the River: Pollution Sources and a Waste Audit
periods.section_ref: What Pollutes Me and Why it Matters
periods.textbook_anchor: What Pollutes Me and Why it Matters — List things thrown into waste bins and describe how each would harm animals, plants, and people if thrown into a river (p. 29)

time_bands.activity: Students look at the textbook images of a polluted river on Textbook p. 28 and name what they see. The teacher asks: 'Where do the plastic wrappers and bags we litter end up?' Students answer from the textbook question on p. 28, sharing reasoning about how litter travels from land to water.

Students make a list of things typically thrown into the waste bin at home and at school — this is the activity on Textbook p. 29. They aim for at least eight items. The teacher notes that both solid waste and liquid waste (soaps, floor cleaners, sewage) pollute rivers, connecting to the question on Textbook p. 28 about home cleaning products.

Students go through their list item by item and write beside each one how it would harm the animals, plants, or people near a river if it entered the water instead of the bin. They categorise: Does it float? Would it dissolve? Would it choke animals? Would it make water undrinkable? The teacher introduces the concept that some pollutants dissolve invisibly while others do not — both cause harm.

Pairs compare their harm descriptions. The class identifies the three items on the collective list judged most dangerous, with reasons. The teacher mentions the Namami Gange programme as an example of organised effort to reverse exactly this kind of damage.

periods.implied_lo: Students can identify sources of river pollution and explain how different types of waste harm aquatic life and human water users.
periods.section_context: Plastic wrappers, bags, litter, waste bin items at home and school, soaps, shampoos, floor cleaners, untreated sewage, factories, soluble vs insoluble pollutants, harm to animals and plants, Namami Gange programme.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask students what cleaning products are used at home and whether they are natural or manufactured — elders in some households still use ash, neem, or clay-based cleaners that are less harmful to water bodies. Draw this out without labelling it; it surfaces intergenerational and regional variation in household practice.

periods.activity_title: Sugar and Oil in Water: A Solubility Inquiry
periods.section_ref: What Pollutes Me and Why it Matters
periods.textbook_anchor: What Pollutes Me and Why it Matters — Add sugar to one glass of water and cooking oil to another, stir, observe, and compare which appears clear (p. 29)

time_bands.activity: The teacher holds up a glass of water and asks: 'If I stir a spoonful of sugar into this, will the water still look clean? What about oil?' Students predict in writing: which will make the water look dirty, and which will seem to disappear?

Groups carry out the activity from Textbook p. 29: one glass gets a spoonful of sugar, one gets a spoonful of cooking oil. Both are stirred well. Students observe and record: What do they see in each glass? Which appears clear? What does the stirred oil do to the surface?

Groups compare observations and discuss: the sugar dissolved and the water looks clear, but is it actually clean? The oil did not dissolve and is visible. Which is more dangerous to fish or someone drinking the water — a pollutant you can see or one you cannot? Students write their reasoning.

Class shares conclusions. The teacher connects findings to fertiliser runoff: dissolved nutrients from fields enter rivers invisibly, but cause algal overgrowth — the 'green blanket' effect — that chokes aquatic life and makes water undrinkable. Students note this connection in their notebooks.

periods.implied_lo: Students can conduct a simple observation inquiry comparing how different substances behave in water and explain what this means for invisible versus visible pollution.
periods.section_context: Clear glasses of water, sugar dissolved in water, cooking oil in water, stirring and observing, which appears clear, soluble pollutants invisible in water, insoluble pollutants visible, fertiliser runoff, algal overgrowth green blanket effect.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Let students attempt the prediction first and commit it to paper — the surprise that clear water may still be polluted is more powerful when their prior guess is recorded. Ask: 'Which kind of pollution is harder for a village that draws water from a river to detect?' to push toward application.

periods.activity_title: Healthy vs Algae-Covered Rivers: Comparing Images and Taking Action
periods.section_ref: What Pollutes Me and Why it Matters
periods.textbook_anchor: What Pollutes Me and Why it Matters — Compare two river images to identify a healthy river and explain what happens when too many plants grow in water, then list three personal actions to protect water bodies (p. 30–31)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook images of a healthy river and an algae-covered river (p. 30)

time_bands.activity: Students open Textbook p. 30 and examine the two river images. Without reading captions, they write: which river looks healthy and why. Responses are shared — students describe colour, clarity, visible life, and surface condition in their own words.

The class reads the section text together. Students answer the three questions from Textbook p. 30: which river is healthy and why, how so many plants can grow in the water (connecting to dissolved nutrients from the previous inquiry), and what happens when too many plants grow. The green blanket effect and its consequences for oxygen, fish, and drinking water are discussed.

Students write their response to the question on Textbook p. 31: three things they personally can do to protect water bodies near them. The teacher asks each student to write at least one action they could start, not just in principle. Groups share and the class builds a collective list on the board.

Students reflect quietly: of the actions listed, which one do they think is hardest to stick to, and why? Two or three students share. The teacher validates that real conservation requires habit change, not just knowledge, and draws out the value of community-level action alongside individual action.

periods.implied_lo: Students can evaluate the health of a water body from observable evidence and identify personal actions that contribute to its conservation.
periods.section_context: Healthy river image, algae-covered river image, green blanket effect, dissolved nutrients causing algal growth, oxygen depletion, harm to fish, undrinkable water, personal conservation actions for water bodies near school or home.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask whether students know a pond, lake, or stream near their home that has become greener or smellier over time — this connects the textbook images to lived observation. Where elders have noticed such changes, that memory is worth surfacing: 'Did your grandparents ever describe the water body as looking different when they were young?'

periods.activity_title: Flood Problems and Preparedness: Matching Impacts and Role-Play Planning
periods.textbook_anchor: When a River Floods — Match flood problems to what each affects (p. 32)

time_bands.activity: The teacher asks: 'Have you or anyone you know ever seen a flood, or seen flood coverage in news? What did it look like?' Students share briefly. The teacher asks what problems a flood would cause in their own neighbourhood — roads, homes, school, food supply.

Students open Textbook p. 32 and complete the matching activity: seven flood problems (dirty water, broken roads, lost crops, no electricity, spread of diseases, damaged homes, schools shut) matched to what each affects (shelter, safe drinking, learning, travel, lights/phones, health, food supply). They record matches in their notebooks and check with a partner.

Students read the Flood Safety Tips infographic on Textbook p. 33, noting actions for before, during, and after a flood. The teacher asks: 'Which of these tips would be hardest to follow? Why?' Students discuss the connection between deforestation and worsening floods — tree cover slows runoff and helps soil absorb water.

Students begin planning their role-play as a Sarpanch or Municipal Corporator from Textbook p. 34 — they write bullet-point notes on four questions: preventing flooding, preventing flood damage, keeping elderly and disabled people safe, and keeping animals safe.

periods.implied_lo: Students can categorise the consequences of a flood across multiple domains of life and identify preparedness actions appropriate to each phase of a flood event.
periods.section_context: Excessive rainfall causing floods, river overflowing banks, dirty water, broken roads, lost crops, no electricity, spread of diseases, damaged homes, schools shut, deforestation and runoff, Flood Safety Tips before/during/after, Sarpanch and Municipal Corporator civic role.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'If you had to leave your home in a flood and could take only three things, what would they be and why?' This grounds the abstract safety tips in a personal decision, and often surfaces what students genuinely value and depend on.

periods.activity_title: Civic Flood Role-Play: Planning Community Disaster Response
periods.textbook_anchor: When a River Floods — Role-play as a Sarpanch or Municipal Corporator planning flood prevention and community safety actions (p. 34)
materials: Notebooks with planning notes from flood matching activity

time_bands.activity: Students review the bullet-point planning notes they wrote in their notebooks during the flood matching and discussion activity. The teacher quickly recaps the four responsibilities: preventing flooding, preventing flood damage, keeping elderly and disabled people safe, keeping animals safe. Groups of four are formed, each group representing one village or town.

Groups conduct the role-play from Textbook p. 34. One student in each group plays the Sarpanch or Municipal Corporator; others play villagers, elderly residents, or a farmer. The group works through their civic plan aloud, speaking as their character and responding to challenges raised by other members — for example, a villager asks where the cattle will go, or an elderly resident asks about medicines.

Two groups share their plans with the class, each in two to three minutes. The class identifies the strongest action from each plan and one gap they noticed. The teacher highlights that real civic preparedness requires both advance planning and community cooperation.

Brief reflection: students write one sentence — 'The most important thing a community can do before a flood is ___' — and share with a neighbour. The teacher closes by connecting deforestation back to prevention: planting trees and protecting forest cover is one long-term civic action.

periods.implied_lo: Students can design and enact a community preparedness plan for a flood emergency, taking the perspective of a civic leader responsible for multiple groups.
periods.section_context: Flood role-play, Sarpanch, Municipal Corporator, village or city civic planning, preventing flooding, preventing flood damage, protecting elderly and disabled people, protecting animals, community cooperation, deforestation and flood prevention.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Let the student playing the civic leader hear challenges from 'villagers' — this is what makes the role-play genuinely evaluative rather than a recitation of tips. If a group finishes their plan quickly, ask: 'What will you do with the animals that cannot be moved?'

periods.activity_title: When Water Runs Out: Scarcity, Adaptation, and Conservation Habits
periods.textbook_anchor: When a River Runs Dry! — Respond to what you would do if there were no water at home for a day and then for a week (p. 35)

time_bands.activity: The teacher reads aloud: 'Imagine waking up and turning on the tap — nothing comes out. Not a drop.' Students are given a moment of quiet thought, then share what they think they would do first. The teacher introduces the Chennai 2019 water crisis and Bengaluru 2022 floods as real examples of cities facing water extremes.

Students write their responses to both questions on Textbook p. 35: what they would do if there were no water for a day, and what they would do if there were none for a week — how they would bathe, drink, cook, clean, and where they would go to find water. Responses are shared in pairs, surfacing how strategies change as scarcity extends.

Class discussion: What habits waste water in daily life? Students list examples — taps left running, full bathtubs, water left in plates. The teacher introduces the National Water Mission and water ATMs as systemic conservation efforts. Students discuss: which conservation actions are individual, which need community coordination, and which need government policy?

Each student commits to one specific water-saving habit they will try — stated as a concrete behaviour, not a general intention. They write it in their notebook. The teacher draws out that drought and water scarcity can force people and animals to migrate, paralleling the earlier discussion of floods.

periods.implied_lo: Students can describe the consequences of water scarcity at personal and community scale and identify concrete conservation behaviours that reduce daily water use.
periods.section_context: No water at home for a day, no water for a week, drinking, bathing, cooking, cleaning without water, finding alternative water sources, Chennai 2019 water crisis, Bengaluru 2022 floods, National Water Mission, water ATMs, individual conservation habits, community and government water conservation.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Has anyone in your family ever had to manage with very little water — during a drought, a pipe burst, or in a village with no piped supply?' Personal accounts of managing scarcity are more instructive than the textbook scenario and connect students to intergenerational resilience practices.

periods.activity_title: Designing a Water Filter: Simple Inquiry with Everyday Materials
periods.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Design a simple water filter using everyday materials and explain what each part does and why (p. 37)
materials: Muddied or coloured water for testing

time_bands.activity: The teacher holds up a glass of muddy water and asks: 'Could you make this safe to look at — or even safer to drink — using only things in this classroom?' Students brainstorm materials freely. The question from Textbook p. 37 is read: 'Can you design a simple water filter using everyday materials? What would you include and why?'

Groups plan their filter on paper before touching materials: they draw a labelled diagram showing the layers or components they will use (e.g. gravel to catch large particles, sand for finer particles, cloth or cotton to trap debris, charcoal if available to absorb colour or odour). Each layer's purpose must be written in the plan.

Groups build their filters using the available materials and test them by slowly pouring a small amount of muddied or coloured water through. They observe and record: Did the water come out clearer? Which layer seemed to do the most work? Did the filter have any limitations?

Groups share findings — showing their filter and comparing the before and after water samples. The class discusses: Does a filter make water fully clean and safe to drink? What more would be needed? The teacher connects this to the chapter's broader theme of humans working with and on rivers to manage water quality.

periods.implied_lo: Students can plan and build a simple multi-layered filter, explain the function of each component, and evaluate its effectiveness through direct observation.
periods.section_context: Designing a water filter, everyday materials, gravel, sand, cotton or cloth, charcoal, muddy or coloured water, filter layers and their purposes, testing filter effectiveness, limitations of simple filtration.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Let groups differ in their layer choices rather than prescribing a single correct design — the comparison of results across groups is itself the inquiry. Ask: 'Why do you think your filter worked better (or worse) than another group's?' to prompt comparative reasoning.

periods.activity_title: Planning a River-Wise City: Synthesis Reflection and River Rule-Making
periods.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Imagine planning a new city near a river and describe steps to keep it clean, prevent floods, and ensure water for all seasons (p. 37)

time_bands.activity: Students read the city-planning prompt from Textbook p. 37: 'Imagine you are planning a new city near a river — what steps would you take to keep the river clean, prevent floods during heavy rains, and ensure there is always enough water for everyone, even in summer?' They spend a moment thinking silently before any sharing.

Students write their city plan in their notebooks, addressing all three dimensions: river cleanliness, flood prevention, and year-round water supply. They may annotate a simple sketch of their city layout if they wish. The teacher circulates and prompts students to draw on specific ideas encountered across the chapter — mangrove conservation, dam trade-offs, deforestation and flooding, the Namami Gange programme, water ATMs.

Students write a response to two of the remaining reflection prompts on Textbook p. 37: the one rule they would create to protect rivers in their city or village, and a time they wasted water and what they could have done differently. Both prompts connect individual agency to systemic change.

A closing sharing circle: each student reads their river rule aloud. The teacher notes patterns — many students may focus on litter, others on industrial waste, others on water rationing — and draws out that protecting a river requires action at individual, community, and government levels simultaneously. The unit closes with the class's collective river rules written briefly on the board.

periods.implied_lo: Students can propose an integrated plan for managing a river-dependent settlement across multiple challenges — cleanliness, flood risk, and water security — drawing on knowledge built across the chapter.
periods.section_context: Planning a new city near a river, keeping river clean, preventing floods, ensuring year-round water supply, one new rule to protect rivers, personal water-wasting reflection, individual and community and government levels of river stewardship.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Which of the three challenges — keeping the river clean, preventing floods, or ensuring enough water in summer — do you think is hardest to solve, and why?' This pushes students toward evaluative reasoning rather than listing. If a student's rule is very general, ask them to make it specific: 'What exactly would happen if someone broke that rule?'

coverage_handoff.section_ref: What Pollutes Me and Why it Matters
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can evaluate the health of a water body from observable evidence and identify personal actions that contribute to its conservation.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Healthy river image, algae-covered river image, green blanket effect, dissolved nutrients causing algal growth, oxygen depletion, harm to fish, undrinkable water, personal conservation actions for water bodies near school or home.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: What Pollutes Me and Why it Matters — Compare two river images to identify a healthy river and explain what happens when too many plants grow in water, then list three personal actions to protect water bodies (p. 30–31)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students compare healthy and algae-covered river images, explain the green blanket effect, list three personal conservation actions, and reflect on which habits are hardest to maintain.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can categorise the consequences of a flood across multiple domains of life and identify preparedness actions appropriate to each phase of a flood event.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Excessive rainfall causing floods, river overflowing banks, dirty water, broken roads, lost crops, no electricity, spread of diseases, damaged homes, schools shut, deforestation and runoff, Flood Safety Tips before/during/after, Sarpanch and Municipal Corporator civic role.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: When a River Floods — Match flood problems to what each affects (p. 32)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students complete the flood-problems matching activity, study the Flood Safety Tips infographic, discuss deforestation's role in worsening floods, and plan role-play notes for civic disaster response.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can design and enact a community preparedness plan for a flood emergency, taking the perspective of a civic leader responsible for multiple groups.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Flood role-play, Sarpanch, Municipal Corporator, village or city civic planning, preventing flooding, preventing flood damage, protecting elderly and disabled people, protecting animals, community cooperation, deforestation and flood prevention.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: When a River Floods — Role-play as a Sarpanch or Municipal Corporator planning flood prevention and community safety actions (p. 34)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Groups role-play as civic leaders planning flood prevention and community safety, enact their plans with character challenges, share with the class, and reflect on the most critical community action.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can describe the consequences of water scarcity at personal and community scale and identify concrete conservation behaviours that reduce daily water use.
coverage_handoff.section_context: No water at home for a day, no water for a week, drinking, bathing, cooking, cleaning without water, finding alternative water sources, Chennai 2019 water crisis, Bengaluru 2022 floods, National Water Mission, water ATMs, individual conservation habits, community and government water conservation.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: When a River Runs Dry! — Respond to what you would do if there were no water at home for a day and then for a week (p. 35)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students write and discuss personal responses to day-long and week-long water scarcity scenarios, identify wasted water habits, and commit to one concrete conservation behaviour.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can plan and build a simple multi-layered filter, explain the function of each component, and evaluate its effectiveness through direct observation.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Designing a water filter, everyday materials, gravel, sand, cotton or cloth, charcoal, muddy or coloured water, filter layers and their purposes, testing filter effectiveness, limitations of simple filtration.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Design a simple water filter using everyday materials and explain what each part does and why (p. 37)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Groups plan and build a multi-layered water filter from everyday materials, test it with muddy water, record results, and discuss limitations and what more would be needed for safe drinking water.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can propose an integrated plan for managing a river-dependent settlement across multiple challenges — cleanliness, flood risk, and water security — drawing on knowledge built across the chapter.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Planning a new city near a river, keeping river clean, preventing floods, ensuring year-round water supply, one new rule to protect rivers, personal water-wasting reflection, individual and community and government levels of river stewardship.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Imagine planning a new city near a river and describe steps to keep it clean, prevent floods, and ensure water for all seasons (p. 37)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students write an integrated city plan addressing cleanliness, flood prevention, and water security; compose a personal river protection rule; reflect on wasted water; and share rules in a closing circle.

assessment_items.question_text: The Godavari river is known as 'Dakshina Ganga' and begins its journey at Trimbakeshwar. Which of the following correctly describes where the Godavari ends its journey?

options.label: A
options.text: It disappears into the Western Ghats before reaching the sea.

options.label: B
options.text: It flows into the Arabian Sea near Mumbai.

options.label: C
options.text: It joins the Bay of Bengal, spreading into a delta.

options.label: D
options.text: It merges with the Ganga river in the north.

assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer is B. A student choosing A confuses the western drainage system (Arabian Sea) with the Godavari's eastward drainage. C indicates a misconception that the Godavari connects to the Ganga, a common confusion about India's major rivers. D indicates a misreading of the source description, applying it to the river's end rather than its beginning.
assessment_items.chapter_section: Where I Begin, Where I Flow
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can extract geographical information about a river system from a map and record its key features.

competency.competency_text: Observes and identifies the natural (insects, plants, birds, animals, geographical features, sun and moon, stars, planets, natural resources) and social (houses, relationships) components in their immediate environment

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student has confused the direction of the Godavari's flow — associating it with the western coast and Arabian Sea rather than the eastern coast and Bay of Bengal.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student has conflated the Godavari with the Ganga, possibly because both are called sacred rivers, without distinguishing their separate courses.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student has misapplied the description of the river's source (Western Ghats) to its endpoint, suggesting they did not trace the river's full path on the map.

assessment_items.question_text: The Godavari is a perennial river. A seasonal river only flows during rainy months. Give two reasons why a perennial river is more valuable to the wildlife and people living along its banks than a seasonal river.
expected_elements: States that a perennial river provides water throughout the year, not only during the rainy season.
Names at least one way year-round water supports wildlife — e.g. animals like tigers, barking deer, or species in the Coringa Mangrove Forests can drink, feed, and breed year-round.
Names at least one way year-round water supports people — e.g. drinking, cooking, irrigation, or fishing can continue in summer and dry months.
assessment_items.annotation: A complete response names continuous year-round flow as the defining feature and links it to at least one wildlife benefit and one human benefit drawn from the section. Accept any wildlife species or ecosystem named in the section (tiger, barking deer, Indian golden gecko, red sandalwood, mangrove). Accept any human use named in the chapter.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can distinguish between perennial and seasonal water systems and explain how year-round flow supports specific wildlife and ecosystems.

competency.competency_text: Identifies natural and humanmade systems that support their lives (water supply, water cycle, river flow systems, seasons, life cycle of plants and animals, food, household items, transport, communication, electricity in the home)

expected_elements: Identifies that perennial rivers flow throughout the year, not only in the monsoon season.
Explains one benefit for wildlife — sustained habitat, drinking water, or breeding conditions — with reference to a species or ecosystem from the section.
Explains one benefit for people — drinking, cooking, irrigation, fishing, or other use — that would be disrupted if the river dried up seasonally.

assessment_items.question_text: Priya lives in a village next to the Godavari. She uses the river every day. List three specific ways Priya and her family depend on the river, and for each way explain what would happen if the river suddenly stopped flowing.
expected_elements: Names three distinct uses from the section — e.g. drinking water, cooking water, washing, irrigation through canals, industrial use, fishing, or farming.
For each use, states a specific consequence of the river stopping — e.g. crops failing, no clean water to drink, fish trade ending.
At least one consequence connects to livelihood or occupation (fishing, farming, ecotourism) rather than only domestic use.
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any three uses named in the section. The consequence for each use should be logically consistent with the use stated — if the student names irrigation, the consequence should relate to crops or food supply. Responses that list three uses but provide no consequences for any of them are incomplete.
assessment_items.chapter_section: The Many Ways I Support Lives
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can identify reasons why human settlements form near water systems and list the ways a river supports daily life and livelihoods.

competency.competency_text: Identifies natural and humanmade systems that support their lives (water supply, water cycle, river flow systems, seasons, life cycle of plants and animals, food, household items, transport, communication, electricity in the home)

expected_elements: Three distinct uses of the river are named — covering at least one domestic use and one livelihood use.
Each use is paired with a specific consequence of the river stopping, not just a general statement about water being important.
At least one consequence addresses livelihoods (farming, fishing, ecotourism) to demonstrate understanding of the river as an economic system, not only a water supply.

assessment_items.task: You have been asked to make a poster for your school entrance showing all the ways rivers help people. Your poster must include drawings and labels for at least five different ways — from homes and farming to boats and jobs. Make your poster in your notebook and be ready to explain one drawing to the class.
assessment_items.scaffold: Think about: What do people at home use river water for? What jobs do people do near rivers? What do farmers need rivers for? Are there any activities on or near rivers besides farming and fishing?
format_of_output: Labelled drawings in notebook — minimum five river uses depicted
At least one drawing from the student's own region alongside textbook examples
Oral explanation of one drawing when sharing
assessment_items.annotation: Assess whether the poster shows at least five distinct uses with intelligible labels. A strong poster includes uses from both the textbook (drinking, cooking, irrigation, fishing, ecotourism) and the student's own regional experience. Accept any locally appropriate uses — region-specific crops, fishing methods, or cultural river uses are valid and encouraged. Do not penalise students whose regions have different staple crops or water-use traditions.
assessment_items.chapter_section: The Many Ways I Support Lives
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can represent multiple human uses of a river system visually and through labelled drawings, connecting textbook content to their own regional context.

competency.competency_text: Identifies natural and humanmade systems that support their lives (water supply, water cycle, river flow systems, seasons, life cycle of plants and animals, food, household items, transport, communication, electricity in the home)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The student can synthesise multiple river uses into a visual product, label each use clearly, and connect textbook content to their own regional context.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold nudges students toward domestic, agricultural, occupational, and recreational uses. A student who uses all four scaffold prompts should produce a varied poster covering the full range of river dependency described in the section.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: five or more distinct uses with clear labels; at least one use drawn from the student's own region; the oral explanation demonstrates understanding of why that use depends on the river. Weak: fewer than five uses; uses that are repetitive (e.g. drinking water drawn three different ways); labels absent or unclear; no regional connection.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who find drawing difficult may write labels with small sketches or symbols. Students who struggle with five uses may be prompted with specific questions: 'What does a farmer need from the river?' 'What do people eat that comes from the river?' Oral explanation of one drawing is an equally valid demonstration of the implied learning outcome.
OPEN_TASK.format_type: Labelled visual poster in notebook with oral component
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The textbook task explicitly calls for a poster with drawings of homes, farms, boats, fishermen and more. The notebook format makes it executable within a single sitting without additional materials.

assessment_items.question_text: A new dam is being planned on a large river in your state. Some people say it will solve water problems; others say it will cause serious harm. Using what you know about how dams work and the problems they can cause, write your view on whether the dam should be built. Give reasons for your answer and suggest at least one way to reduce the harm the dam might cause.
look_for: Accurately describes what a dam does — stores river water in a reservoir by blocking flow.
Names at least two benefits — water supply for drinking, irrigation, or electricity generation.
Names at least two problems — flooding of land, displacement of wildlife, displacement of people.
Takes a reasoned position that acknowledges both sides rather than presenting only benefits or only harms.
Proposes at least one specific measure to reduce harm — e.g. relocating and compensating displaced communities, creating wildlife corridors, limiting dam size.
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any reasoned position — for, against, or conditional — provided it is supported by specific benefits and harms from the section. Do not penalise students who reach a different conclusion from others, so long as they demonstrate understanding of the trade-off. The harm-reduction measure must be specific; a general statement that 'we should be careful' is insufficient for full marks.
assessment_items.chapter_section: Dams—Storing My Water, Changing My Flow
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can identify the benefits and costs of a human-made water storage structure and reason about trade-offs between development and displacement.

competency.competency_text: Demonstrates how natural resources can be shared, maintained, and conserved (trees, use of rainwater, benefits of millets)

look_for: Demonstrates understanding of how a dam functions — blocks river flow, creates a reservoir, stores water.
Lists at least two concrete benefits (drinking water, irrigation, electricity) and two concrete problems (land flooded, wildlife displaced, people relocated).
Shows genuine reasoning about the trade-off — the response engages with both sides rather than stating only one.
Takes a position with stated reasoning, not just a list of pros and cons.
Proposes at least one specific, actionable harm-reduction measure drawn from the logic of the section.

assessment_items.question_text: Rajan throws plastic bags into the drain outside his school every day. His teacher says this harms the river nearby. Which of the following best explains HOW the plastic from the drain ends up harming fish in the river?

options.label: A
options.text: Rainwater carries the plastic from drains into the river, where fish may eat it or get trapped in it.

options.label: B
options.text: The plastic blocks sunlight above the drain, making the water in the drain too cold for fish.

options.label: C
options.text: The plastic dissolves in water like sugar and makes the river water too sweet for fish to breathe.

options.label: D
options.text: The plastic makes the drain water taste different, so less water flows into the river.

assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer is B. A student choosing A has confused a sensory property (taste) with a physical mechanism and shows no understanding of how litter travels to water bodies. C places the problem in the drain rather than the river and introduces an implausible mechanism. D confuses the solubility of sugar (from the inquiry activity) with plastic behaviour — plastic does not dissolve — indicating a direct misconception from the solubility experiment.
assessment_items.chapter_section: What Pollutes Me and Why it Matters
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can identify sources of river pollution and explain how different types of waste harm aquatic life and human water users.

competency.competency_text: Identifies natural and humanmade systems that support their lives (water supply, water cycle, river flow systems, seasons, life cycle of plants and animals, food, household items, transport, communication, electricity in the home)

what_each_option_reveals.D: The student has not understood how litter physically travels from land to water; they are guessing at a sensory mechanism rather than a transport pathway.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student has confined the problem to the drain and introduced an implausible sunlight-cold water mechanism, showing they have not grasped how land-based pollution enters rivers.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student has directly misapplied the solubility inquiry result — transferring what sugar does (dissolves) to plastic, which does not dissolve, indicating a specific misconception to address.

assessment_items.question_text: In the solubility activity, one glass of water had sugar stirred into it and another had cooking oil stirred into it. Both glasses looked different after stirring. Answer the following: (a) Which glass looked clearer after stirring — the sugar water or the oil water? (b) Is the clearer water necessarily safe to drink? Explain why or why not. (c) What does this tell us about one type of river pollution that is hard to detect?
expected_elements: States that the sugar-water glass appeared clearer because the sugar dissolved and became invisible.
Explains that clear water is not necessarily safe — dissolved pollutants like fertilisers or chemicals cannot be seen but still harm people and aquatic life.
Connects the invisible-but-harmful pollutant idea to fertiliser runoff entering rivers and causing algal overgrowth (green blanket effect) or making water unsafe to drink.
assessment_items.annotation: Part (a) has a single correct answer — the sugar water looked clearer. Parts (b) and (c) require reasoning. Accept any scientifically sound explanation of why dissolved pollutants are dangerous even when invisible. The connection to fertiliser runoff and algal overgrowth is the expected textbook link, but accept any chemically coherent example of an invisible river pollutant.
assessment_items.chapter_section: What Pollutes Me and Why it Matters
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can conduct a simple observation inquiry comparing how different substances behave in water and explain what this means for invisible versus visible pollution.

competency.competency_text: Performs simple inquiry related to specific questions independently or in groups

expected_elements: Correctly identifies the sugar-water glass as appearing clearer and explains that sugar dissolved into the water.
States clearly that clear-looking water can still be unsafe because dissolved substances are invisible but may be harmful.
Makes a specific connection to real river pollution — fertiliser runoff, algal growth, or another dissolved pollutant that renders water unsafe or damages aquatic life.

assessment_items.task: Look at the two river images described below in words. River A: clear blue-green water, fish visible below the surface, birds on the banks, children swimming. River B: a thick green mat covers the entire water surface, no fish visible, a bad smell, no animals near the water. Write three sentences explaining which river is healthier and why. Then write three things you personally will do — starting this week — to make sure the river or water body nearest to you does not become like River B.
assessment_items.scaffold: For the comparison: Think about what the green mat is made of, why it grows so thick, and what happens to the oxygen and animals underneath it. For your personal actions: Choose actions you can actually do at home or school — not just rules for others to follow.
format_of_output: Three written sentences comparing River A and River B and explaining the cause of River B's condition
Three personally committed conservation actions written as first-person statements
assessment_items.annotation: The text-based river descriptions replace a printed image, keeping the item self-contained. A strong response names the green blanket (algal overgrowth) by cause — fertiliser runoff or excess nutrients — not just by appearance. Personal actions must be specific and first-person (e.g. 'I will not throw soap water into the drain' rather than 'people should not pollute'). Accept any locally appropriate conservation action. Region-specific water bodies, local pollution sources, or traditional water-conservation practices mentioned in the personal actions are valid and should be valued.
assessment_items.chapter_section: What Pollutes Me and Why it Matters
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can evaluate the health of a water body from observable evidence and identify personal actions that contribute to its conservation.

competency.competency_text: Demonstrates how natural resources can be shared, maintained, and conserved (trees, use of rainwater, benefits of millets)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The student can interpret observable signs of a water body's health, explain the mechanism behind deterioration, and translate that understanding into specific personal conservation commitments.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The first scaffold prompt guides students to move beyond 'River B looks dirty' toward naming the cause — excess algal growth from dissolved nutrients. The second prompt redirects students away from policy statements toward personal, executable actions.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: River B's condition is explained by naming algal overgrowth and its cause (nutrient runoff); three specific first-person conservation actions are stated with enough detail to be executable this week. Weak: comparison stops at appearance ('River B is green and smelly') with no causal explanation; personal actions are vague or written as rules for others rather than commitments.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who cannot write three full sentences may draw River A and River B side by side with labels explaining the difference, and state their conservation actions orally. Students whose nearest water body is a pond, well, or canal rather than a river should apply the same reasoning to that water body.
OPEN_TASK.format_type: Written comparison and personal commitment list
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The textbook task compares two images and asks for personal conservation actions — this item replicates that task in a text-based, self-contained format executable within a single sitting.

assessment_items.question_text: Heavy rains cause a river to flood a village. The Flood Safety Tips say people should move to higher ground during a flood. Which of the following explains WHY deforestation in the hills above the village makes flooding worse?

options.label: A
options.text: Without trees, rain clouds form faster over the hills and produce even more rain.

options.label: B
options.text: Without trees, rainwater runs quickly over bare soil into the river instead of being slowed down and absorbed.

options.label: C
options.text: Without trees, the river has no shade and the water gets warmer, which makes it overflow.

options.label: D
options.text: Without trees, the wind blows harder and pushes more river water onto the land.

assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer is B. A student choosing A has introduced a cloud-formation mechanism not present in the section, indicating they are guessing rather than reasoning from the textbook's runoff explanation. C shows a confusion between river temperature and overflow — a plausible-sounding but incorrect causal chain. D introduces wind as a flooding mechanism, showing the student has not grasped the soil-absorption and runoff explanation in the section.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can categorise the consequences of a flood across multiple domains of life and identify preparedness actions appropriate to each phase of a flood event.

competency.competency_text: Discusses how to prepare for emergency situations (smoke, fire, small injuries, burns, electrical safety, unseasonal rains, fallen trees) based on discussions with family and community, or personal experiences

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student has invented a cloud-formation mechanism to explain the deforestation link, showing they have not understood the soil-absorption and runoff explanation in the section.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student has confused river temperature with overflow, introducing a plausible-sounding but textbook-unsupported causal chain.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student has introduced wind as a flooding mechanism, indicating they have not engaged with the section's explanation that tree cover slows runoff and helps soil absorb water.

assessment_items.task: You are the Sarpanch of a village that floods badly every monsoon. Write a short plan (four to five sentences) for what your village will do BEFORE the monsoon begins to prevent damage and keep everyone safe. Your plan must include at least one action for elderly people or people with disabilities, and at least one action for animals.
assessment_items.scaffold: Think about: What can the village do before the rains start — not just during the flood? Who in the village needs extra help to get to safety? How can you protect animals that cannot move themselves?
format_of_output: Written plan of four to five sentences in the voice of the Sarpanch
At least one action for elderly people or people with disabilities named explicitly
At least one action for animals named explicitly
assessment_items.annotation: The student is being asked to apply flood preparedness knowledge in a civic leadership role, as practised in the role-play activity. A strong response focuses on before-monsoon preparation (not just during-flood reaction), includes specific vulnerable groups, and demonstrates understanding that preparedness is a community-level responsibility. Accept any locally plausible flood prevention or preparedness actions — region-specific flood experiences or traditional community practices for flood readiness are valid and should be valued.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can design and enact a community preparedness plan for a flood emergency, taking the perspective of a civic leader responsible for multiple groups.

competency.competency_text: Discusses how to prepare for emergency situations (smoke, fire, small injuries, burns, electrical safety, unseasonal rains, fallen trees) based on discussions with family and community, or personal experiences

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The student can translate flood preparedness knowledge into a civic plan that considers multiple groups — the general community, elderly or disabled residents, and animals — and that focuses on proactive preparation rather than only reactive response.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold explicitly redirects students from during-flood responses (which are instinctive) toward before-monsoon preparation (which requires planning). The prompts about who needs extra help and how to protect animals prevent students from producing a generic 'move to higher ground' plan.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: focuses on pre-monsoon actions; names specific groups (elderly, disabled, animals) with specific provisions; reads as a plan, not a list of safety tips. Weak: describes only what to do during a flood; names vulnerable groups without any specific provision for them; does not demonstrate a leadership perspective.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who find extended writing difficult may present their plan as a numbered list of five actions with brief labels. Oral presentation of the plan to the teacher is an equally valid demonstration if writing is a barrier. Accept plans modelled on any civic leadership structure the student is familiar with — Panchayat, municipal committee, school safety committee.
OPEN_TASK.format_type: Short written civic plan in first-person voice of civic leader
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The role-play activity that produced this implied learning outcome required students to think and speak as civic leaders — the written plan in that voice is the most direct text-based demonstration of the same competency.

assessment_items.question_text: In 2019, Chennai faced a severe water crisis when its reservoirs ran dry. Millions of people had no tap water for weeks. (a) Describe two serious problems people would face in daily life during such a crisis. (b) Explain two things individuals, families, or communities can do regularly to prevent such a crisis from happening again. (c) Why is water conservation important not just for individuals but for everyone in a city or village?
look_for: Names two specific daily-life problems arising from water scarcity — covering at least two domains such as drinking, cooking, hygiene, health, or livelihoods.
Proposes two concrete, regular conservation actions at individual, family, or community level — not one-time events.

Explains the collective dimension: why individual conservation alone is insufficient and why community-level or government-level coordination (National Water Mission, water ATMs, or equivalent) is also needed.
Uses specific detail from the section rather than only general statements about the importance of water.
assessment_items.annotation: Part (a) should draw on the p. 35 scenarios (bathing, drinking, cooking, cleaning without water, finding alternative sources). Part (b) should reflect concrete conservation habits discussed in the unit. Part (c) should articulate a shared-resource argument — water is a collective resource whose depletion affects everyone, making individual conservation insufficient on its own. Accept any reasonable real-world examples from the student's region alongside the Chennai and National Water Mission references from the textbook.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can describe the consequences of water scarcity at personal and community scale and identify concrete conservation behaviours that reduce daily water use.

competency.competency_text: Demonstrates how natural resources can be shared, maintained, and conserved (trees, use of rainwater, benefits of millets)

look_for: Two specific daily-life problems are named with sufficient detail to show understanding of what water scarcity actually prevents people from doing.
Two conservation actions are concrete and regular — not one-time interventions — and are executable at individual, family, or community level.

The collective dimension is explicitly addressed: the student demonstrates understanding that water is a shared resource whose depletion affects everyone, and that community-level and government-level action complements individual effort.
The response uses specific detail — a named city, a named government programme, or a specific conservation behaviour — rather than only general claims about water being precious.

assessment_items.question_text: Your class is building a simple water filter using sand, gravel, cloth, and charcoal. (a) Name the correct order in which you would arrange these materials in the filter, starting from the top where muddy water enters. (b) Explain what job ONE of the layers does. (c) After the muddy water passes through your filter, would you say it is safe to drink? Explain your answer.
expected_elements: Gives a plausible layering order — e.g. gravel or coarse material at top to catch large particles, followed by sand for finer particles, then cloth or cotton, then charcoal; the specific order may vary as long as the reasoning is sound.
Explains the function of one named layer accurately — e.g. gravel catches large debris, sand filters finer particles, charcoal absorbs colour or odour, cloth traps small particles.

States that filtered water is not necessarily safe to drink because small dissolved pollutants, bacteria, or chemicals may still be present — the filter removes visible particles but not all contaminants.
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any layering order that is physically justified — the grading from coarser to finer is the key principle, but students who reverse it and explain why are demonstrating reasoning. Part (c) is the critical thinking component: a student who says 'yes, it is safe to drink' without qualification has not grasped the inquiry's closing conclusion that simple filtration has limits.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can plan and build a simple multi-layered filter, explain the function of each component, and evaluate its effectiveness through direct observation.

competency.competency_text: Performs simple inquiry related to specific questions independently or in groups

expected_elements: A physically plausible layering sequence is given, with coarser materials before finer ones as the general principle — accept reasonable variation if the student can justify it.
One layer's function is explained accurately and specifically, not just named.
The student explicitly states that filtered water is not fully safe to drink and gives a reason — bacteria, dissolved chemicals, or other contaminants that filtration cannot remove.

assessment_items.question_text: Imagine you are helping plan a new town that will be built beside a river. The town will have 10,000 families. Write a plan explaining: (a) three steps you would take to keep the river clean as the town grows; (b) two steps to prevent floods during heavy rains; (c) one step to make sure there is enough water for everyone even in a dry summer. For each step, explain why it matters.
look_for: Three river-cleanliness steps are proposed with reasons — e.g. treating sewage before release, banning plastic near the river, creating buffer green zones, organising community clean-up, limiting factory discharge.

Two flood prevention steps with reasons — e.g. planting trees or restoring forest cover to slow runoff, building drainage systems, not constructing on flood plains, maintaining mangrove or riparian vegetation.
One water security step with a reason — e.g. building a small reservoir, harvesting rainwater, implementing a water rationing system, installing water ATMs, mandating conservation practices.
Each step is paired with an explanation of why it matters — the student demonstrates understanding of the causal connection, not just the action.
The plan draws on multiple sections of the chapter — cleanliness from the pollution section, flooding from the floods section, water security from the drought and dams sections.
assessment_items.annotation: This item assesses integration across the chapter's major themes. A strong response does not simply list facts from separate sections but shows how the three challenges are connected — e.g. a student who notes that forest cover both prevents floods and recharges groundwater for summer use is demonstrating cross-section synthesis. Accept any locally appropriate planning measures — region-specific flood management, traditional water harvesting structures, or local conservation practices are valid.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can propose an integrated plan for managing a river-dependent settlement across multiple challenges — cleanliness, flood risk, and water security — drawing on knowledge built across the chapter.

competency.competency_text: Demonstrates how natural resources can be shared, maintained, and conserved (trees, use of rainwater, benefits of millets)

look_for: Three distinct cleanliness steps are proposed, each with a causal explanation — not just a list of good practices.
Two flood prevention steps are given with reasons rooted in the relationship between land cover, runoff, and river overflow — not just 'build a wall'.
One water security step is proposed with a reason that connects seasonal scarcity to a structural or behavioural solution.
The explanations demonstrate causal understanding — the student shows why each step matters, not just what should be done.
The plan reflects thinking across multiple chapter themes — pollution, flooding, and drought — rather than focusing on only one.
